t:
Clause (c) of section 106 of the Agricultural Act of 1949, as amended, is amended to read as follows:

“(c) 
If acreage poundage or poundage farm marketing quotas are in effect under section 317 or 319 of the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938, as amended, (1) price support shall not be made available on tobacco marketed in excess of 110 per centum of the marketing quota (after adjustments) for the farm on which such tobacco was produced, and (2) for the purpose of price-support eligibility, tobacco carried over from one marketing year to another shall, when marketed, be considered tobacco of the then current crop.”

fable.w: This section only sets substantive price-support eligibility rules for tobacco when marketing quotas are in effect. The tempting reading is that marketing quotas under the 1938 Act involve farmer referenda, but referenda are excluded by the definition and none is provided for in this section. There is no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government.
fable.s: price support shall not be made available on tobacco marketed in excess of 110 per centum of the marketing quota (after adjustments) for the farm on which such tobacco was produced

opus.w: This amendment sets rules for when tobacco can get price support: no support for tobacco marketed above 110% of the farm's quota, and carried-over tobacco counts as part of the current crop. It gives no role to anyone outside the federal government. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, or right to sue. Marketing quotas can be connected to farmer referenda elsewhere in the law, but no referendum is mentioned here, and referenda don't count as participation anyway.
opus.s: price support shall not be made available on tobacco marketed in excess of 110 per centum of the marketing quota (after adjustments) for the farm on which such tobacco was produced
opus.b: Some readers might be tempted to answer "Yes" because tobacco marketing quotas under the 1938 Act are tied to farmer referenda, and the word "marketing" suggests outside parties are involved. That reading fails for two reasons. The section doesn't mention any referendum, and the definition excludes referenda in any case. All the section does is set when tobacco is eligible for price support.

qwen_chat.w: This section defines eligibility criteria for price supports based on existing marketing quotas. It does not establish a process for public participation, consultation, or comment in the creation or modification of those quotas. The text describes administrative rules for benefit eligibility, which falls under the exclusion for 'applications for benefits' or general regulatory provisions without external input mechanisms.
qwen_chat.s: If acreage poundage or poundage farm marketing quotas are in effect under section 317 or 319 of the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938, as amended, (1) price support shall not be made available on tobacco marketed in excess of 110 per centum of the marketing quota (after adjustments) for the farm on which such tobacco was produced, and (2) for the purpose of price-support eligibility, tobacco carried over from one marketing year to another shall, when marketed, be considered tobacco of the then current crop.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the mention of "marketing quotas" implies a process where farmers participate in setting those quotas. However, this specific section only defines the consequences of exceeding those quotas (loss of price support) and how carryover tobacco is treated. It does not describe the process for establishing the quotas or any mechanism for public input into that decision. The text is purely regulatory/administrative regarding eligibility for benefits.
